analysis.one_liner: Restores pandemic emergency paid sick and family leave until the federal COVID emergency ends.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in May 2021 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The emergency paid leave program Congress created in early 2020 — paid sick leave for workers who caught COVID-19 or had to care for someone who did, plus emergency family leave — was written to expire on December 31, 2020. This bill would have brought it back and kept it running until the Health and Human Services Secretary declared the COVID-19 public health emergency over. Employers would again have had to provide the leave, with federal tax credits covering most of the wage cost.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — including millions without employer-provided sick leave — who get sick with COVID-19, are quarantined, or need to care for a sick family member. They would be able to stay home without losing pay, which also reduces pressure on sick people to go to work and spread infection. Employers who comply would be reimbursed for the wages through tax credits.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the emergency paid sick leave benefit and extends its availability until the end of the declared COVID-19 public health emergency, rather than its earlier December 31, 2020 expiration date.
Restores the emergency family and medical leave provision tied to the pandemic, which also had lapsed on December 31, 2020.
Changes the leave entitlement so the annual paid sick time cap applies in each calendar year, rather than limiting it to a single one-time use.

analysis.who_pays: Employers must provide and pay for the leave up front, though federal tax credits refund most of the wage cost; the federal treasury bears the cost of those credits. Businesses also carry the administrative burden and the risk of staffing gaps when workers use leave.

drawbacks.text: Employers bear the cost and disruption of providing leave while workers are out, and the tax credit reimbursement arrives after the fact, which weighs most heavily on small employers with tight cash flow.

The extension runs to an open-ended end date — whenever the Secretary of Health and Human Services declares the emergency over — giving businesses no fixed deadline to plan around, and the emergency ultimately lasted into 2023.

The bill would revive a program that had already been allowed to lapse more than four months before it was introduced, when the bulk of pandemic workplace disruption had passed and many workers had no access to it for the worst later waves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is real and direct: paid time off when infected or caregiving, which protects both family finances and public health. The costs are genuine but partially offset — tax credits refund employers for most wage costs, and the scope is limited to the length of the declared emergency. The bill's main design weakness is its open-ended expiration and the fact that, by the time it was introduced, the original program had already been dead for months.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees in May 2021, but no committee ever acted on it and it died at the end of the 117th Congress in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Foster introduced the Pandemic Leave Extension Act on May 7, 2021, with eight colleagues joining the introduction.
The Speaker referred it to three committees — Education and Labor, Oversight and Reform, and House Administration — for a period to be subsequently determined.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed the referral.

The bill's original targets, the emergency paid sick leave and family leave provisions, had expired on December 31, 2020, so the leave it would restore was already unavailable when the bill was filed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would otherwise have had to provide and administer the leave are better off, along with the federal treasury, which avoided the cost of the reimbursement credits. Workers who caught COVID-19 or cared for family members after 2020 without paid leave absorbed that cost themselves.

for.name: Rep. Bill Foster
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 7, 2021 to restore and extend the expired pandemic paid leave programs.

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the Education and Labor, Oversight and Reform, and House Administration committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after its referral in May 2021.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to three committees for later consideration and never brought it to the House floor in the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported it and the bill never drew opposition votes because it was never brought to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have re-imposed a mandate to provide paid leave to sick or caregiving workers, though federal tax credits would reimburse most wage costs. The industry's interest in avoiding the mandate runs against workers' interest in paid leave, but the reimbursement blunts the cost.
Extending the employer tax credits for paid leave wages would add federal spending for the remainder of the declared emergency; in return, workers get the leave itself.
